title: Idempotency keys and duplicate request handling
description: Protect payment and mutation endpoints from accidental double-submits. Learn idempotency keys, storage strategies, and how to make unsafe HTTP methods safe to retry.

data.text: Network glitches, impatient users, and aggressive retry logic all create the same problem: the same mutation can arrive twice. Without protection, a customer may be charged twice, two identical records may be created, or inventory may be decremented twice. Idempotency keys are the production answer to this class of bug.

An idempotency key is a unique value the client sends on the first request. The server stores the result keyed by that value. If the same request arrives again, the server returns the stored result instead of re-executing the business logic.

The standard pattern is the `Idempotency-Key` header. The client generates a new UUID for every new action and reuses the same UUID if it retries. The server checks whether it has seen that UUID before.

items: Client sends `POST /payments` with `Idempotency-Key: abc-123` and the order payload.
Server checks the idempotency store for `abc-123`.
If not found, the server executes the payment, stores the result with `abc-123`, and returns 200.
If found, the server returns the stored 200 response without re-processing.
If a request is still in progress, the server returns 409 Conflict or 429 to prevent parallel duplicates.

data.text: The store must be durable and atomic. A relational database table is usually sufficient. You need the request payload hash, the resulting status code, the response body, and an expiry timestamp. Use a unique constraint on the key so concurrent requests for the same key cannot create duplicates.

data.title: Idempotency record model

data.text: The cleanest implementation is a middleware that sits before your controllers. It reads the header, locks the key, checks the store, and either short-circuits with the cached response or allows the request to proceed and records the outcome.

data.title: Idempotency middleware

data.text: Two retries can arrive at the server simultaneously for the same key. Without locking, both will see no record and both will execute. Use a distributed lock—Redis `SET key value NX EX 10` is a common choice—so the first request claims the key, others wait briefly, and then read the cached result.

data.title: Critical detail
data.text: The lock must expire. If a request crashes after acquiring the lock, a permanent lock deadlalls all future retries for that key. Always set a short TTL.

Not every endpoint needs idempotency. Reserve it for financial transactions, order creation, and any state-changing action where duplicates are dangerous. Read-only endpoints are naturally idempotent. Safe methods like GET and DELETE do not need this header, though DELETE can benefit from a key if the delete itself is expensive or irreversible.

data.title: Key takeaways
items: Idempotency keys protect mutation endpoints from duplicate execution caused by retries.
Store the key, request hash, status, and response body durably with a unique constraint.
Use a distributed lock with a short TTL to prevent parallel duplicates.
Require the key only on endpoints where duplicates would be harmful.
